A."],"published-print":{"date-parts":[[2009,2,8]]},"abstract":"<jats:p>\n                    While closed timelike curves (CTCs) are not known to exist, studying their consequences has led to non-trivial insights into general relativity, quantum information and other areas. In this paper, we show that, if CTCs existed, quantum computers would be no more powerful than classical computers: both would have the (extremely large) power of the complexity class polynomial space (\n                    <jats:inline-formula>\n                      <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\/\/www.w3.org\/1999\/xlink\" xlink:href=\"631equ6.gif\"\/>\n                    <\/jats:inline-formula>\n                    ), consisting of all problems solvable by a conventional computer using a polynomial amount of memory. This solves an open problem proposed by one of us in 2005, and gives an essentially complete understanding of computational complexity in the presence of CTCs. Following the work of Deutsch, we treat a CTC as simply a region of spacetime where a \u2018causal consistency\u2019 condition is imposed, meaning that nature has to produce a (probabilistic or quantum) fixed point of some evolution operator. Our conclusion is then a consequence of the following theorem: given any quantum circuit (not necessarily unitary), a fixed point of the circuit can be (implicitly) computed in\n                    <jats:inline-formula>\n                      <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink=\"http:\/\/www.w3.org\/1999\/xlink\" xlink:href=\"631equ7.gif\"\/>\n                    <\/jats:inline-formula>\n                    . This theorem might have independent applications in quantum information.\n                  <\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.1098\/rspa.2008.0350","type":"journal-article","created":{"date-parts":[[2008,11,13]],"date-time":"2008-11-13T17:54:01Z","timestamp":1226598841000},"page":"631-647","update-policy":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.1098\/crossmark-policy","source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":65,"title":["Closed timelike curves make quantum and classical computing equivalent"],"prefix":"10.1098","volume":"465","author":[{"given":"Scott","family":"Aaronson","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of TechnologyCambridge, MA 02139, USA"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"John","family":"Watrous","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"School of Computer Science, University of WaterlooWaterloo, Ontario, Canada N2L 3G1"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"member":"175","published-online":{"date-parts":[[2008,11,11]]},"reference":[{"key":"e_1_3_2_2_1","doi-asserted-by":"crossref","unstructured":"Aaronson S. 2005 NP-complete problems and physical reality.
